I served 21 years in the Marine Corps as an infantry officer with 3 years in combat.

As a platoon commander in Vietnam (1968-1969) I can honestly say that I've never met a woman, civilian or Woman Marine, who could have endured what we had to The combat loads were much heavier than in training, we carried less food in order to carry more ammunition, we were in the field in combat for up to one or two months without getting back to battalion and some hot chow, we stunk to high heaven without bathing for so long, our uniforms literally rotted off after a few weeks in the monsoons, on combat patrols you don't scurry off in the bushes to relieve yourself--you do it where you stand, crossing rice paddies always meant massive ring worm infestations and leaches, resupply was unreliable so one C-Ration (theoretically you rate 3 a day) had to last 2-3 days, no potable water so we filled canteens with whatever was available (rice paddy water as a last resort) and put water purification tablets in to try to kill most of the critters, the water often stunk, I probably had diarrhea 10 out of the 12 months, the few times we got back to battalion for a hot meal, the food was so rich by comparison to the C-Rations that it made many Marines (including me) sick.

You don't get more than a few hours of sleep a day. You learn to just lay down in the mud in a driving rain to get an hour or so of sleep.

You often wonder if you will see the sunset each day or the sunrise each night. It wears on you mentally. But the mines were the worse. In some areas we were in they were everywhere.

There were good days when miracles happen. In one frontal assault across a dry rice paddy under heavy automatic fire, I didn't think half my platoon would make it to the treeline. But when the fight was over, I had one slightly wounded Marine and we had killed 21 North Vietnamese soldiers.

There were really bad days that change your life forever. One day when the sun rose, I had 34 Marines in my platoon (including me). When the sun set that day, only 4 of us were still alive and unwounded, but still holding our ground.

This doesn't include the mental and physical exhaustion of continuous combat over long periods. Firefights, mines, booby-traps, friendly fires, death, horribly wounded, chaos, carnage, and fear.

And I don't think women are strong enough to carry casualties off the field of battle with all of their combat gear and not having time to take the combat load off the wounded. Adrenaline surely helps, but the difference in strength and body weight make it nearly impossible for her to get a wounded Marine to safety under fire.

In 1968 during training, we were required to low crawl 100 yards in full combat gear, lift up a Marine simulating a casualties with his full combat gear and in a fireman's carry, get him 100 yards back to "safety." Our "evil" instructors always paired the smaller Marines with the hulks pretending to be wounded. I remember I got paired with a linebacker who had played for the Philadelphia Eagles who was my "casualty." I weighed 160 at the time and he weighed over 200. Dear God, the one and only thing that got me back to the "finish" line was the fear of failing.
